title: Forgiveness, Feasting, and the Lord of the Sabbath
summary: Back in Capernaum, Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man lowered through a roof, provoking scribes who say only God can forgive sins. He calls Levi the tax collector and eats with tax collectors and sinners, explains why his disciples do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, and defends his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, declaring that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
story: Chapter 1 showed Jesus' authority over evil spirits and disease, and ended with crowds pressing in from everywhere. Chapter 2 turns to conflict. Religious teachers now watch Jesus closely and object to what he says and does: he claims to forgive sins, he keeps company with the wrong people, his disciples do not fast, and they break Sabbath rules. This is the first of a series of five controversy stories that runs to 3:6, where the Pharisees and Herodians begin plotting to destroy him. Already, very early in the Gospel, the shadow of the cross falls across the story, and in verse 20 Jesus speaks of the day the bridegroom will be taken away.
historical:
The chapter is still set in Galilee in the late 20s AD, under Herod Antipas. Antipas collected revenue through local tax farmers who bid for the right to collect tolls and duties, and Capernaum, on a road near the border between Antipas's territory and his brother Philip's, was a natural place for a toll booth. Tax collectors like Levi were widely despised, both as collaborators with the ruling powers and because the system invited them to collect more than was owed and keep the difference. Levi is called Matthew in the parallel account (Matthew 9:9).

The scribes and Pharisees who appear here were not the temple rulers but teachers of the law and members of a renewal movement concerned with purity, tithing, and the Sabbath. Their concerns were serious attempts to keep God's law faithfully in daily life. David's eating of the consecrated bread, which Jesus cites, is told in 1 Samuel 21:1-6, where the priest at Nob is Ahimelech; his son Abiathar later became David's high priest and the better known figure. The difficulty this raises is taken up under the hard question below.
cultural:
Village houses in Galilee often had flat roofs made of wooden beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair, so digging through one to lower a mat was possible, though it would have made a mess of someone's home. Meals were shared lying on couches or mats, and eating with someone signaled acceptance and friendship. Sinners in the Gospels means people known for breaking the law, or whose way of life placed them outside the circle of the observant, and eating with them risked one's reputation and, some thought, one's purity.

The law of Moses commanded only one annual fast, on the Day of Atonement, but devout Jews added voluntary fasts; Luke 18:12 mentions a Pharisee who fasted twice a week. The Sabbath, the seventh day, was set apart for rest (Exodus 20:8-11), and teachers defined which activities counted as work. Picking a few heads of grain from a neighbor's field was allowed on ordinary days (Deuteronomy 23:25), but on the Sabbath it could be classed as reaping, one of the kinds of work later Jewish law explicitly forbade. The consecrated bread was the twelve loaves set out each week before the Lord in the sanctuary and afterward eaten by the priests (Leviticus 24:5-9).
literary: The chapter contains four of the five controversy stories that run from 2:1 to 3:6. Each has a similar shape: an action by Jesus or his disciples, an objection, and a decisive saying from Jesus. Many scholars have noticed that the five stories are arranged in a symmetrical pattern: the first and last are healings that raise questions about Jesus' authority (forgiveness, the Sabbath), the second and fourth involve eating, and the central one, about fasting, contains the first hint of Jesus' death. The healing of the paralytic is itself a story within a story, broken off in the middle of a sentence (verse 10) as Jesus turns from the scribes to the man. The sayings about patches and wineskins use everyday images to show that Jesus brings something new that cannot simply be added to old patterns.

outline.t: A paralyzed man forgiven and healed
Levi called; Jesus eats with sinners
The question about fasting: bridegroom, patch, and wineskins

doctrines.note: Jesus declares a man's sins forgiven before he heals his body, showing that forgiveness is the deeper need. He says he came to call sinners, not the righteous: salvation is for those who know they are sick and need a doctor.

The scribes are right that only God can forgive sins. Jesus does not deny it; he demonstrates that the Son of Man has this authority on earth. He also claims to be Lord of the Sabbath, the day God himself instituted.

Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath but restores its purpose: it was made for human good, not humans for it. His appeal to David shows that the law itself recognizes human need and has a place for mercy.

words.note: Aphiemi, to release, let go, or forgive. The basic sense is to send away or release, as a debt is canceled. When Jesus tells the paralytic his sins are forgiven, he uses a passive form that points to God as the forgiver, and yet he speaks with God's authority, which is what the scribes find blasphemous.

Hamartolos, sinner, someone who misses the mark. In the Gospels it often labels a social group, people seen as openly disregarding the law, often paired with tax collectors. Jesus accepts the label as a description of those he came to call and does not accept it as a reason to keep away.

Nesteuo, to fast, going without food as a sign of mourning, repentance, or devotion. Jesus does not reject fasting; he says his presence is a time of celebration like a wedding, and that his disciples will fast when the bridegroom is taken away, which Christians have observed ever since.

Sabbaton, Sabbath, from a Hebrew word meaning to cease or rest. The Sabbath was a sign of the covenant between God and Israel and a weekly remembrance of creation and of freedom from slavery in Egypt. It becomes the focus of conflict in this chapter and the next.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus doing what God alone does. He forgives sins, and proves his authority by healing. He calls himself the bridegroom, a role the Old Testament gives to God in his covenant love for Israel (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2:19-20). He claims to be Lord of the Sabbath. The title he uses, Son of Man, appears here for the first time in Mark; it could simply mean a human being, but it also recalls the figure in Daniel 7 who receives authority from God. Yet this authority is exercised in mercy: at a table full of tax collectors, and on behalf of hungry disciples. The hint in verse 20 that the bridegroom will be taken away points already to the cross, where his authority to forgive will be secured.

hard.q: Jesus says David ate the consecrated bread when Abiathar was high priest, but 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech. Is this a mistake?
hard.a: The difficulty is real, and Matthew and Luke both leave out the name when they retell the story, which suggests they noticed it. Several answers have been offered. One reads the Greek phrase as a way of referring to a section of Scripture, meaning in the passage about Abiathar, since Jews often referred to passages by a key name; Mark uses a similar phrase at 12:26, in the passage about the bush. Another notes that Abiathar was present at Nob, survived the massacre that followed (1 Samuel 22:20), became high priest under David, and was far better known, so the phrase can mean in the days of Abiathar, who later held the office, rather than naming the officiating priest. A third suggests confusion in the tradition, since the Old Testament itself mixes the names of Ahimelech and Abiathar elsewhere (2 Samuel 8:17). Some scholars simply judge it an error by Mark or his source. Readers differ in how they weigh these, and the point of Jesus' argument, that human need and God's purpose stand behind the law, is unaffected.

questions: Four friends carried the paralyzed man and dug through a roof, and Jesus saw their faith. Who has carried you toward Jesus, and whom might you carry?
Jesus ate with people others avoided. What would it look like for your table, or your church's, to be as open as his?
The Sabbath was made for man. How do you rest, and how might you receive rest as God's gift rather than as a rule or an afterthought?
